newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pushes ahead with Mideast summit plans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pushes ahead with Mideast summit plans.

text.p: Brushing aside Arab pleas for a postponment, the United States on Monday pressed ahead with plans to convene an emergency Middle East summit to try to restore peace between Israel and the Palestinians.
"We expect the meeting that the president announced yesterday (Sunday) to proceed," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
His comment came after Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak asked U.S. President Bill Clinton to postpone the summit set for Tuesday in Washington.

Arafat and Mubarak met for more than two hours on Monday in the northwest Egyptian town of Burg al-Arab, and Arab diplomats said they wanted assurances a summit would bring firm guarantees of Israeli gestures toward the Palestinians.
But after U.S. signals that delaying the summit was out of the question, a Palestinian official said Arafat would go to Washington after talks in Luxembourg with European ministers.
"He is going now to Luxembourg and then Washington," the official, who declined to be identified, said in Cairo.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and King Hussein of Jordan accepted their invitations and were reported to have left for Washington on Monday.
But Mubarak's participiation remained in doubt, a U.S. official said.
Asked if Clinton had any commitments that the Washington meeting would produce substantive results, McCurry said:

"These talks are occurring without preconditions, but based on the president's conversations yesterday, he hopes and expects the leaders to arrive in a frame of mind to make progress on the issues that divide them."
Clinton proposed the summit to help end bloody fighting that erupted in the West Bank and Gaza last week after Israel opened an archaeological tunnel near Islam holy places in Jerusalem.
Fifty-five Palestinians and 14 Israels had been killed by Monday in five days of clashes.

Clinton is trying to keep a fragile peace agreement between Israel and the Palestinians from unravelling in the midst of the U.S. presidential campaign. He cleared his calendar through the middle of the week to act as mediator.

One of the highlights of Clinton's presidency was his shepherding of Arafat and the late Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin into a "historic handshake" at 1993 White House ceremonies in which Israel and the Palestinians signed a peace accord designed to end a long and bloody feud.

"Priorities are priorities. The Middle East peace process is at a very difficult, important moment ... and the president felt it important to concentrate his energies on bringing the parties together," McCurry said.

He said the summit would be a success if Netanyahu, head of a right-wing Israeli government in office only a little more than three months, and Palestinian leader Arafat agree "to do everything within their power to end the violence ... (and) show a renewed commitment to address their differences in the negotiations."
The timing of the meeting was critical for Clinton not only of the Middle East stakes but because of an upcoming milestone in the U.S. presidential race.
Clinton is scheduled to hold the first of two campaign debates with Republican challenger Bob Dole in Hartford, Connecticut, next Sunday, and planned to begin preparing for the encounter on Thursday.
